frameworks.name: The 5 Opening Archetypes
frameworks.summary: A decision rule for choosing the shape of your opening - question, story, contrarian claim, startling statistic, or scene - based on the room's state and the raw material you actually hold.
steps: State the room's state in one line: confident, worried, or indifferent. This determines the job the opening has to do.
Name the job: create stakes, resolve a dispute, or establish a person. An opening that tries to do two jobs does neither.

Inventory what you actually hold, honestly: a story you lived, a contrary claim you can defend, a number you can cite with its denominator, a question the room is already arguing about, or a person you can name.
Select the archetype whose raw material you hold. If you are reaching for a statistic you cannot source, use a scene instead.
Draft the opening in 20 seconds. Then check the friction: does it contain a handle someone could quote, a small surprise, and a stake tied to this audience?
Name the payoff the opening promises, and confirm you will deliver it in the talk. An opening is a contract with the room.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it for every talk where the room does not already know you and trust you, which is most keynotes, all-hands, and first meetings. Skip the formal process for recurring internal updates where the audience is already on your side - there, open with the decision and move on.
frameworks.example: A founder is opening a 30-minute keynote at a 1,200-person industry conference. The room's state is confident and slightly bored - three well-funded competitors are in the audience. The job is to create stakes, because the audience does not yet know there is a problem worth their attention. The raw material inventory: no verified industry statistic she can source, one customer story with a genuine turn, and a defensible contrary claim about how the category is run. She chooses the contrarian claim, opens with 'Every vendor in this room will tell you the bottleneck is implementation. It isn't - it is who is allowed to say no', and follows with the customer story as proof. She does not use a statistic, because she cannot source one, and a sourced-but-irrelevant number would have cost her the room.

frameworks.name: The Open Loop
frameworks.summary: A four-step method for planting one unresolved question with a promised payoff, and closing it visibly so the audience experiences resolution.
steps: Name the question the room is already asking but nobody has said out loud - usually the one behind the decision they have been asked to make.
Phrase it as a specific, answerable question with an object at the end of it, not a rhetorical question and not a sentiment.
Plant it in the first ninety seconds, in the audience's language, and promise the payoff explicitly: 'by the end of this, I will tell you which of these three we should bet on'.
Narrow it once in the middle of the talk, so the audience feels it closing rather than waiting passively.
Close it visibly in the final minutes, using the same words you opened with, and give the answer as a decision or a fact rather than as 'it depends'.
Audit before you present: every question asked in the first two minutes must be answered out loud somewhere in the talk.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it in talks of eight minutes or more where you must hold attention and where you genuinely have an answer. Do not use it in three-minute updates, and never use it when you do not know the answer - in a room of executives, an open loop that resolves into hedging is the most expensive mistake available to you.
frameworks.example: A COO opens a quarterly business review with: 'The reason our best customer churned in June is a decision we made in March, and I have not told any of you what that decision was yet. By the end of this I will tell you what it was and what I am changing about how we make that class of decision.' The question is specific, the payoff is promised with a timeframe, it is narrowed halfway through, and it is closed explicitly in the final slide with the same framing. The board knows from minute one what the talk is about, and the mid-talk narrowing keeps them with it.

frameworks.name: The Callback Close
frameworks.summary: A method for ending a talk by returning to the opening image, question, or phrase and giving it new meaning, so the talk reads as a single arc.
steps: Write three candidate closing lines, each a complete sentence you would be content to be quoted on.
Choose the shared element - an image, a question, or a short phrase - that will connect the close to the open.
Go back to the opening and make sure the element is planted with enough concrete detail to be recalled: a number, an object, a named person.
Write the middle so the element is never explained. An explained image is a lecture; an unexplained one is a motif.
In the close, re-use the element in a new context so that it now means something it did not mean before. One line only.
Run the seam test: read the opening and the closing alone, back to back. If they stand alone as a message, the arc works.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it for keynotes, narrative talks, and anything over eight minutes where you want the audience to leave with an image as well as an argument. Skip it for short technical briefings, compliance updates, and any room where plainness is the dominant value - a forced callback in a boardroom reads as a trick.
frameworks.example: A sales leader opens a user conference keynote with a photograph of a customer whiteboard covered in handwritten numbers, and the line 'Ninety-four percent of this board is a workaround'. She does not explain the board, and she returns to it only in the final two minutes, when the company's new pricing and support change means that 94 percent of those workarounds disappear - the number on the board is now the number of people no longer writing it. The callback is a single line, the same image, and a changed meaning. The audience reports the whiteboard for months, not the pricing slide.

frameworks.name: The Last-Line Test
frameworks.summary: A four-question check on the final sentence of a talk that determines whether the ending carries meaning or merely ends.
steps: Write the final sentence alone on a card, with no other context around it.
Ask: would this sentence still make sense if the speaker never appeared again, and would the room be able to repeat it tomorrow?
Reject 'thank you', 'so that's it', 'any questions', 'I'm excited to share this' and 'let's get started' as last lines. Thanks and questions belong earlier in the close.
If the last line is the ask, write it as an imperative with a named person, a named action, and a date attached. If the last line is the image, make sure the ask was already delivered.
Rehearse the last three sentences verbatim, standing, more than any other part of the talk - it is the part you will be most tempted to rush.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it on every talk, without exception, and apply it twice: once when you draft and once after you have delivered the talk, when the distance will show you the line you actually said versus the one you meant to say.
frameworks.example: A product founder's talk ends: 'So, that's the strategy. Thank you - any questions?' Written on a card alone, the line has no subject, no stake, and no verb the audience can act on. It fails the test twice over. The rewritten last line is: 'If we ship the enterprise tier by the fourteenth, we do not need a second sales office - and I am asking for four engineers and one legal review to make that date.' The first version is pleasant and forgettable; the second is arguable, dated, and repeatable, and it is the version the customer repeats to their CFO on the drive home.

frameworks.name: The Ask Formula
frameworks.summary: A six-part structure for making an explicit, dated, consequential ask - the difference between a talk that ends and a talk that changes something.
steps: Name the one person or body who must act. 'Everyone' is not a person and never moves.
Name the action as a verb: approve, sign, hire, introduce us to, stop, fund.
Attach the size or scope: the amount, the headcount, the number of calls, the length of the commitment.
Attach the date: 'by the fifteenth', 'before Tuesday's board', 'in the next two weeks'. An undated ask is a wish.
State what they get, in their terms, so the ask is a trade rather than a demand.
State what happens if they do not act - honestly, without threat - because a consequence is what makes a date real.
frameworks.whenToUse: Use it in every talk that requires a decision, and in the closing of a renewal or negotiation call, where an unstated ask is usually read as a lack of confidence. Do not use it for speeches that require nothing, and do not stack two asks - two asks is no ask. The structure is a course synthesis drawn from basic decision hygiene and from Chris Voss's calibrated questions ('How am I supposed to do that?'), which invite the other side to solve for the constraint rather than argue against you.
frameworks.example: A founder asking a Series A lead investor to lead a 4 million dollar round. The ask: 'We need you to lead - 3 million of your own money at a 25 percent discount, with a wire by the 22nd, and we will send the data room on Monday.' The size, the discount, the date, the deliverable, and the consequence (an extended runway plan and a slower hire) are all in one sentence. Compare with 'We would love you to consider leading this round' - which identifies no person, no amount, no date, and no consequence, and is the reason a founder waits four months for an answer they already asked for.

scenarios.title: The keynote you have lost four minutes of
scenarios.setting: A 1,200-person industry conference. You are the founder, on the main stage, booked for 28 minutes. The panel before you overran, so the stage manager tells you at the wings that you have 24 and will be cut off hard. You need to announce a pricing change that will annoy half the room, and you need a 200-person trial to fill the sales pipeline for the quarter.
scenarios.challenge: You have to open, hold a room that is already slightly irritated by the delay, deliver a pricing change people will not like, and close with a CTA - in 24 minutes rather than 28.
objectives: Open with something that survives a slightly hostile, time-pressured room
Land an unpopular change without hiding it
Close with one specific, dated ask rather than a general invitation

options.text: Open with 'Thanks for your patience - sorry we're running a little over. Before I get into the announcement, let me give you a quick bit of background on how we got here and what the product does today.'
options.outcome: You have spent the room's peak attention on an apology and a primer, in a room that has already been held past its limit. By the time you reach the pricing change, the room has classified the talk as a vendor update and the announcement lands as a surprise rather than as a considered position.
options.feedback: This is the throat-clearing tax in full, and you are paying it in a room that is already behind. Acknowledge the time pressure in a single clause, then go straight to the thing they came for. The pricing change is the stake - it belongs in the first thirty seconds, not at minute six.

options.text: Open with the contrarian claim ('Most teams in this category are priced for the buyers' best quarter, not their worst'), back it with a customer result you can name, then present the pricing change as the consequence of taking that position, and close with the trial ask.
options.outcome: The room gets a position to disagree with, which is more engaging than a primer, and the pricing change arrives as an argument rather than as an announcement. The ask lands last and is the only thing the room can act on.
options.feedback: This is the right shape for a room you must convert. The change is controversial, so it needs an argumentative frame - do not present it as a decision you made, present it as a bet you are making and can defend. Check the twenty-four minutes: the claim plus the customer proof is about four, the change is about eight.

options.text: Open with a startling statistic from an industry report you read that week, then move to the pricing change.
options.outcome: The number buys a beat of attention and then turns into a liability: someone in the front rows asks whether you can source it, and you cannot. You spend the next ninety seconds of a hostile-feeling room on defending a number that was never yours, and the pricing change is delayed into the middle.
options.feedback: A statistic you cannot source is a cost centre. If the number comes from your own customers or your own data, use it and name the denominator. If it comes from a report, either source it or replace it with the customer story you can defend.

options.text: Open with a scene - one customer, on a call, watching a competitor's pricing page - and let the pricing change fall out of the scene.
options.outcome: The scene is vivid and the room settles, but it is slow to pay off and you have lost four minutes already. You arrive at the pricing change at minute seven, having spent the highest-attention window on a story that does not yet have a point.
options.feedback: A scene can absolutely carry this talk, but it needs the point inside the first thirty seconds and it needs to be short. If you use the scene, cut it to two details, and make the point of the scene explicit before the pricing change appears.

scenarios.coachingNote: In a compressed slot with a room already aggrieved, the opening must do two things at once: give them a position to hold and get out of the way. Deciding which archetype you can actually source is the first decision; protecting the first ninety seconds from your own preamble is the second.

scenarios.title: Four thousand people, one difficult announcement
scenarios.setting: A 4,000-person all-hands, mostly remote, streamed to offices in six countries. You are announcing the closure of the Austin site, affecting 120 people, many of whom are in the room. The CEO is in the second row. Phones are out. You have 25 minutes and no script.
scenarios.challenge: You must open, deliver the news, and close, knowing that every word is being recorded and forwarded, and that a weak close on this one will be the thing people quote for years.
objectives: Open in a way that does not spend the room's trust before you have asked for it
Deliver the news without hiding it and without performing remorse
Close with something specific and human rather than corporate

options.text: Open with the quarter's wins - revenue, launches, customer logos - and mention the Austin closure in the final section.
options.outcome: Every one of the 120 affected people recognises the tactic within a minute, and so does everyone else. The closure becomes a buried item rather than a managed one, and the rest of the talk is read as company spin. The people who received the news last feel second-hand in a room that was supposed to be about them.
options.feedback: Bad news is not softened by sequencing; it is only made less controllable. Whatever the order, this news reaches the room with more force if it comes from you first and with the specific detail attached. Put it in the first two minutes.

options.text: Open by naming the decision plainly, say who it affects and when, acknowledge that it is bad news without apologising for the company, then give the specifics of what happens to people, and close on the one thing you will personally guarantee.
options.outcome: The room gets the information in the order it needs it: what, who, when, what happens, what I will do. Nobody has to guess whether they heard it correctly. The close lands because it is a commitment rather than a summary.
options.feedback: This is the standard, and it is mostly about resisting the urge to add context. A market rationale is fine - one sentence - and it should come after the news, not before it. The guarantee at the end should be something you control personally, and it should be small enough to be true.

options.text: Open with the market context - why the industry is contracting - and let the closure emerge from the analysis.
options.outcome: The room hears a rationalisation, and rationalisations read as excuses to people who already know they are being made. The analytical frame also eats eight minutes you do not have, and the announcement arrives in the last third when attention is lowest.
options.feedback: Analysis is the speaker's comfort zone and the audience's least favourite part of a hard announcement. Facts about the market do not reduce the cost to 120 specific people. Lead with the decision, then one sentence of cause, then the human detail.

options.text: Open with a thank-you to the Austin team by name, then deliver the closure, then close with a general commitment to 'support everyone through this transition'.
options.outcome: The thank-you reads as a preamble to bad news, which makes the news feel like a betrayal of the sentiment rather than a decision. The closing commitment is generic enough to be true and specific enough to be worthless, and the affected employees - who are now live on a recorded stream - hear a promise that names no person, no date, and no action.
options.feedback: Gratitude can lead an announcement, but only if it is specific and unconnected to the decision. And the close must be concrete: name what happens for the 120 people, by when, and who is accountable. 'Support everyone through the transition' is a slogan; 'every person in Austin will have a call from their manager by the end of this week, and a written plan within two weeks' is a commitment.

scenarios.coachingNote: When the news is bad, the order of information is the whole job: decision, people affected, timing, cause, remedy, and one specific commitment. Every instinct to bury, contextualise, or soften the first sentence costs you the room's trust in the last one.

scenarios.title: The renewal call with a stranger in the room
scenarios.setting: A $340,000 annual renewal, eleven days from decision. On the call are a new VP of Operations who has never met you and a procurement manager who has pushed for concessions. You have 30 minutes; your champion - the original buyer - forwarded the invite and is not on it. The VP opens with 'we have some questions about the last two quarters'.
scenarios.challenge: You must open the call, survive a hostile opening, and close with a specific commercial ask - a two-year commitment with a small expansion - while a procurement professional is actively looking for a discount.
objectives: Open in a way that re-establishes relevance with a room that does not know you
Neutralise the 'questions about the last two quarters' opening without defensiveness
Close with one dated ask rather than a summary of value

options.text: Open with a recap of the last twelve months of product releases, your roadmap, and how the platform has performed for other customers in their industry.
options.outcome: You have answered a question nobody asked, in a language the new VP does not yet share, with evidence they cannot use. The procurement manager uses the time to note everything they will negotiate, and the two problems - the churn risk and the contract length - are still exactly where you left them.
options.feedback: Your history is not their outcome. Everything you say about releases and other customers is unusable by a room whose problem is 'why did the last two quarters go badly'. Lead with their outcome, then with what you need from them.

options.text: Open by labelling the concern out loud ('It sounds like what you actually want to know is whether this is safe to renew for another year at a higher price, given what you saw in Q2'), answer the underlying question with specific evidence, and close with the two-year ask and a decision date.
options.outcome: You have taken the objection off the table before it hardened, demonstrated that you understood their situation, and turned the call from a status update into a decision. The procurement manager has nothing to negotiate against because the conversation was never about price.
options.feedback: This is Chris Voss's labelling applied to a commercial call, and it is the highest-leverage thirty seconds available. Name the real worry, in their words, before they spend energy on it. Then the ask: a term, an amount, and a date by which you need the answer.

options.text: Open with a customer story about a company in the same industry that had a similar problem and fixed it with your product.
options.outcome: The story is relevant and it works - the new VP leans in - but it is someone else's outcome and this is a room that has just told you your results were inadequate. You have made the customer feel like a case study, and the procurement manager is now looking for a reason to discount.
options.feedback: A peer story is a good second beat, provided it is short and the first thing you said was still their own situation. Lead with their outcome, then use the peer story as proof, and never let the story run long enough to look like a case study.

options.text: Open with 'Before we get into the details, I want to give some context on the product' and end the call with 'Thanks for your time - we will follow up with the paperwork'.
options.outcome: The call ends without a commitment, a term, or a date. The renewal is now 'in progress', which in a procurement organisation means it goes into a queue and gets reviewed against two other vendors who did ask for a decision. The competitor who asked is already signed.
options.feedback: The closing is the failure here, not the opening. A call that ends without a named next step, a date, and a signature path will be lost to a competitor that asked. Use the Ask Formula: who signs, what they sign, by when, and what happens if we do not have it by the 15th.

scenarios.coachingNote: In a renewal with a new stakeholder, your credibility has to be rebuilt from their outcomes in the first sixty seconds, and your ask has to be on the table before the procurement team can set the agenda. The call does not end when you stop talking; it ends when they know what they are deciding and by when.

scenarios.title: The toast that has to work
scenarios.setting: Your mother-in-law's 40th anniversary dinner. About 70 people - her family, your business partner, and the investor who asked you to 'tell the story of how it started' without ever having said it. You have three minutes, after the main course, with a glass in your hand. Your mother-in-law has privately told you she thinks your decision to leave your job and start a company was a mistake.
scenarios.challenge: You need to toast the couple, signal to a room that includes your business partner and an investor that you are credible, without turning a family dinner into a pitch or embarrassing the woman who is hosting you.
objectives: Land the emotional stakes of the occasion before anything else
Rhyme the opening and the closing so the three minutes feel like a whole thing
Make one small, specific ask rather than a grand statement

options.text: A formal tribute: a few slides about the couple read from your phone, listing the years, the children, and the qualities that make them special.
options.outcome: The room tunes out somewhere in the second paragraph of the list, and the three minutes feel long. The person who matters most is being described rather than celebrated, and nothing in the toast is memorable enough to survive the week.
options.feedback: Lists of attributes are not a toast. A toast is one story, one image, one turn. Also: never read from a phone at a family table - the light, the angle, and the fact that everyone can see the screen all work against you.

options.text: A long, warm story about your partner, ending with a genuine tribute, with no joke and no reference to the announcement.
options.outcome: The room enjoys it and nobody remembers it, because there is no handle and no turn. Your mother-in-law is charmed and the investor hears nothing that tells them anything about you - which is fine, because this is a dinner, but it is a wasted evening for the career conversation you did not have.
options.feedback: A warm story is the right shape; it just needs a specific, concrete detail that only you would know, and a last line that lands as a statement rather than a summary. Warmth is not a substitute for a point.

options.text: A short story about the moment you told your mother-in-law you were leaving your job to start the company - what she said, and what it cost you - ending on the couple, with one specific, small ask of the room.
options.outcome: The moment you name is the one she is most curious about and the one nobody at that table has heard, so the room leans in. She is included rather than managed, the room gets something true about you, and the ask - a small, concrete, slightly funny request that only the people at the table can grant - gives the toast a shape and a landing.
options.feedback: This works because it is a callback structure in miniature: an image at the start, a changed meaning at the end. Two things to protect: keep her dignity (do not narrate her doubts in front of 70 people) and keep the ask small, warm, and specific - a toast that ends in a business request will undo everything before it.

options.text: A charming, slightly risky joke about your mother-in-law, followed by a short passage about what you have learned about commitment from the couple.
options.outcome: The joke gets a laugh from her family and a wince from her, which is exactly the outcome the evening did not need. The tribute that follows is decent and slightly apologetic, and it never quite recovers the room's warmth.
options.feedback: Humour at a family table works only if the target is yourself or a shared situation, never the person honouring you. If you want a joke, aim it at your own circumstances, and make sure the punchline does not require anyone in the room to be the butt of it.

scenarios.coachingNote: The same architecture that runs a keynote runs a toast: an image, a turn, a callback, a landing, and one ask. What changes is only the stakes of getting it wrong and the amount of time you have. Write the last line first, make the detail something only you know, and be careful who you are making the subject of the story.

scenarios.title: Twelve minutes to land a funding decision
scenarios.setting: A board meeting of a seed-stage company. You have a twelve-minute slot for one agenda item - a request to approve a bridge round of $1.2 million at a 30 percent discount, with a hard decision needed today because an investor's term sheet expires at 5pm. The CEO is supportive but visibly sceptical of the discount. Two board members have not read the memo.
scenarios.challenge: You must open, make the case for a pricing decision that will cost the team real money, and close with a request for a vote - in twelve minutes, to a room that is behind.
objectives: Open in a way that gets the behind board members oriented without wasting the slot
Make the case for a bad-looking commercial trade honestly
Close with a specific motion the board can actually vote on

options.text: Open with a walk through the full metrics deck - growth, burn, runway, pipeline, cohort retention - before you get to the ask.
options.outcome: The behind board members are oriented and the board is bored, because they can already see where this is going and they have seen the metrics. You arrive at the ask with four minutes left, which means you rush it, and a rushed ask in a boardroom is read as a rushed request.
options.feedback: The metrics belong in the case, not in the opening. Lead with the decision, then give the two numbers that matter, and keep the rest in the appendix. A board that trusts your numbers does not need them narrated in order.

options.text: Open with the decision, the amount, and the reason the discount is the right trade; state the one thing you are uncertain about; make the case in three minutes; close by asking for a specific motion, with a time limit.
options.outcome: The board is oriented in the first thirty seconds, the honest uncertainty buys credibility rather than costing it, and the close is a motion somebody can say yes or no to. The vote happens today, which was the whole point.
options.feedback: This is the shape for any board ask: decision, amount, reason, the honest uncertainty, the case, the motion. Naming the uncertainty is what keeps a sceptical director from deciding the whole thing on tone.

options.text: Open with a customer story about the flagship account that is expanding, and close with 'as you can see, the market is large and growing'.
options.outcome: The story is good and it is irrelevant to the vote, because the directors are not being asked whether the market is large - they are being asked whether to give up 30 percent of the company. The close confirms that you did not notice the question, and the motion is deferred to the next meeting, by which time the term sheet has expired.
options.feedback: Match the evidence to the decision. The board is not evaluating the market; they are evaluating a trade. Give them the trade: what the discount buys in runway and in certainty, what it costs, and what happens if you do not take it.

options.text: Open with a rhetorical question to the room - 'Are we really going to let a term sheet expire over three hundred thousand dollars?' - and pause, letting the silence do the work.
options.outcome: The silence is excruciating for everyone except you, and the board does not take the bait; directors do not fill rhetorical silence with agreement, they fill it with a counter-question about why you needed the discount at all. You have invited the objection on your worst ground and handed the room the frame.
options.feedback: Never open a boardroom on a question you cannot answer. If you are confident enough to pose the question, you should be confident enough to answer it before they do, and you should answer it yourself rather than inviting the answer.

scenarios.coachingNote: A board ask is not a talk; it is a decision with a receipt. Everything before the motion is the case, everything after it is implementation. Write the motion first, in the exact words you want recorded, and build backwards from it.

exercises.title: The three-opening reel
exercises.instructions: Choose one talk you are genuinely giving in the next month. Write three openings for it: one question, one story or scene, and one contrarian claim. Each must carry the same stake - the same consequence for the audience - so the only variable is the shape. Keep each to 90 seconds and record all three on video, standing, without notes. Then play them back in order and mark, for each: the exact second the stake appears, whether you can name the archetype, and whether the audience could repeat one sentence from it tomorrow. Bring the three recordings and your marked timings to the session.
exercises.deliverable: Three recorded 90-second openings of the same talk, plus a one-line note on each identifying the archetype, the second the stake lands, and the handle you would want repeated.
successCriteria: All three openings carry an identical stake, so the comparison is about shape rather than content.
Each opening lands its stake within the first 30 seconds, and the exact second is written down for each.
Each opening is a single archetype with no hybrid elements, and you can name which one it is.
Each opening contains one handle - a number, a name, or a specific image - that could be repeated by an audience member.
You have identified which of the three you would actually use, and you can say why in one sentence that refers to the room rather than to your preference.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Here is the deal: three takes, ninety seconds each, and the stake stays identical in all three so we are comparing shapes and not content. Record them standing and without notes, because a scripted opening hides the thing we are looking for. When you have all three, tell me which archetype you gravitate to by default, because that is usually the one you are worst at - and we will work out which of the three this room actually needs.

exercises.title: The live first ninety seconds
exercises.instructions: Pick a real meeting in the next 72 hours where a decision is expected - a one-on-one, a team review, a customer call. Do not prepare a deck and do not present. In the 60 seconds before you begin, write the stake and the archetype you are using on a card. Open with that, and with nothing else: no agenda, no context, no throat-clearing. Keep the open to 90 seconds. After the meeting, write three lines: the second the room engaged, the first thing they said back, and whether the loop or ask you planted was still live in their questions. Then bring the card and the three lines to the session.
exercises.deliverable: A pre-meeting card with the stake and the archetype, the delivered opening, and a three-line retrospective on engagement and whether the plant survived.
successCriteria: The opening was 90 seconds or less and contained no agenda, background, or credentials.
The card was written before the meeting, not reconstructed afterwards.
The retrospective cites what the room actually said or did, not what you felt about their attention.
You can state whether the room repeated or referred back to your stake at any point, with evidence.
You name one sentence from your natural opening that you cut, and whether cutting it changed anything.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: This one runs on a real meeting, so let us get the card right before you walk in. Tell me who is in the room, what decision is pending, and what you actually have to work with - a story, a number, a claim, a question they are already asking. Then we will write a 90-second opening on one card that you can hold in your hand. The moment you get back, I want the three lines, especially the part about whether they picked the stake up or ignored it.

exercises.title: The open-and-close autopsy
exercises.instructions: Take the most recent real talk you delivered of five minutes or more - a recording if you have one, otherwise a transcript or a colleague's notes. Play it at 1.5x with a pen and mark four timestamps: when the stake first appears, when the room's likely attention would have decayed if the stake had not landed, where you plant a question you never answer, and the exact final sentence. Then count the seconds of preamble before the stake, and write down what the last sentence of the talk actually was, word for word. Produce a one-page autopsy: the four timestamps, the preamble count, the last line quoted, and two specific rewrites - one new first sentence and one new last sentence. No general overhaul.
exercises.deliverable: A one-page autopsy with four timestamps, the preamble seconds counted, the last line quoted verbatim, and two rewritten lines.
successCriteria: Every claim is anchored to a timestamp from the recording or transcript, not to recollection.
The preamble count is a real number of seconds, and at least one preamble sentence is quoted and marked for deletion.
The final sentence is quoted word for word and passed or failed against the Last-Line Test explicitly.
The two rewrites are specific sentences, not descriptions of what to do.
The autopsy names one thing the recording proves that your memory got wrong.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: This is an autopsy, so expect it to sting in a useful way. Send me the recording, or a transcript with timestamps if that is all you have. We are marking four moments only - stake, decay point, dangling question, last line - and counting your preamble seconds. Then we write two new lines and nothing else. Resist the urge to redesign the whole talk; the ends are what we are fixing.

exercises.title: The last-line test in the room
exercises.instructions: Write five candidate last lines for a talk you are giving, and put each on its own card with nothing else on it. Record yourself delivering each card as if it were the end of the talk, cold, with no preamble - ten seconds each, five takes. Then ask one person who is not preparing a talk to listen to the five takes in a random order and, after twenty minutes, write down the sentence they remember. You will get a score. Compare it with the line you thought was strongest and write one paragraph on why the winner won.
exercises.deliverable: Five written last lines, five recorded ten-second deliveries, and a written result from the listener's twenty-minute recall test with your analysis of the winning line.
successCriteria: All five lines are complete sentences that would work with no other context.
At least one line is an explicit ask with a person, an action, and a date attached.
The listener's recall is recorded verbatim, and the winning line is not always the one you predicted.
The analysis explains the winning line in terms of concreteness, stake, or self-relevance rather than 'it felt better'.
You have rewritten your chosen last line once, tightening it by at least three words.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Five cards, ten seconds each, no preamble - and then we get a real score from a real listener after twenty minutes, which is the only honest test of a last line. The interesting result is usually the one you did not predict, so do not tell me your favourite before the listener writes theirs down. Once we have the result, we will tighten the winner by at least three words and rehearse it standing.

exercises.title: Land the ask in a real decision
exercises.instructions: Identify a real conversation in the next week where a decision is genuinely pending from someone else - a budget, a hire, a contract, a scope change. Write the ask using the six parts of the Ask Formula: who acts, the action, the size, the date, what they get, and what happens if they do not. Deliver it in the final 60 seconds of the meeting, as a standalone sentence, and then stop talking. Do not soften it, do not add a second ask, and do not re-explain it if they ask a clarifying question. After the meeting, record or obtain a note of the other side's actual response, in their words, and bring that to the session along with your ask card.
exercises.deliverable: A written six-part ask card, the delivered ask in a real meeting, and a verbatim record of the other side's response.
successCriteria: The ask card names a specific person or body, a specific action, a size or scope, and a date.
The ask was delivered in the final 60 seconds as a standalone sentence, with no speech before or after it.
No second ask was made, and no explanation was added after delivery.
You have the other side's response in their own words, not your summary of it.
The retrospective names one part of the formula that made the ask land and one part that you think weakened it.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: We will write the ask card now, all six parts, before you go into the meeting. The two things I will hold you to: it goes in the last sixty seconds as one standalone sentence, and then you stop talking - no softening, no second ask, no explanation afterwards. When you come back, bring the other side's actual words rather than your impression of them, because the gap between those two is where the learning is.

exercises.title: The archetype sprint
exercises.instructions: Set a timer and run five rounds of 4 minutes. In each round, pick one archetype from the 5 Opening Archetypes, and deliver a 90-second opening for a real talk you have coming up, with the stake held constant across all five rounds. Do not write anything down beforehand - improvise, but begin each attempt with the stake named aloud so the shape is what varies. At the end of each round, note in one line which archetype you were strongest in and which was hardest to do without rambling. Then pick one archetype you refuse to use, and write one line explaining why you will not use it in the next six months - or what would have to be true for you to use it.
exercises.deliverable: Five timed 90-second improvised openings across the five archetypes, with a one-line note per round and a written statement of which archetype you are ruling out and why.
successCriteria: All five rounds are timed at 90 seconds and delivered without notes, with the stake named at the start of each.
Each attempt is a single archetype, and you can name which one you were doing while it was happening.
You notice a difference in how long the archetypes take - stories and scenes overrun, questions and claims finish early.
You have written the line on the archetype you are ruling out, and it references a specific condition rather than a preference.
You have identified which archetype you are most likely to default to under pressure, and what that reveals about your style.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: Twenty minutes, five rounds, one archetype each, ninety seconds apiece, and the stake stays fixed so we are testing shapes. Keep it rough - improvised openings are supposed to be a bit rough, that is where the edges show. When we finish, I want your read on which one you are strongest in and which one you would normally skip, because that is usually the archetype your room needs most.

exercises.title: Write the rhyme
exercises.instructions: Take a real talk you will give in the next eight weeks and work backwards. Step one: write three candidate last lines, each a complete sentence you would be content to be quoted on. Step two: choose the shared element - an image, a question, or a short phrase - and write the first sentence of the talk for each candidate. Step three: choose the pair and run the seam test - read only the opening and the closing, back to back, with nothing in between, and judge whether they work as a two-line message. Step four: check that your plant in the opening is concrete enough to be recalled, and that the payoff in the closing changes the meaning of it. Then write the one place in the middle of the talk where you will narrow the open loop.
exercises.deliverable: A one-page document with three candidate last lines, the three matching first sentences, the chosen pair, the seam-test result written out, and the mid-talk loop-narrowing sentence.
successCriteria: The three candidate last lines are complete, quotable sentences with no dependence on the talk around them.
Each candidate has a matching first sentence, and the chosen pair shares exactly one element.
The seam test result is written out as a verdict with a reason, not as a feeling.
The plant in the opening is concrete enough to be recalled by someone who was not looking at a screen.
The mid-talk narrowing sentence is written in the room's language, not yours, and it narrows rather than merely references the loop.
exercises.liveCoachPrompt: We are working backwards, which is the part people skip: the closing comes first, and the opening is written to make it inevitable. Give me the talk, the audience, and the one thing you want them to walk out believing, and we will write three last lines first. Then we will test the chosen pair with the seam test, because that test is what tells you whether you have a spine or a list.

assessment.title: The 90-second opening and the 30-second close
assessment.brief: You will deliver a 7-minute talk to a panel drawn from your real target audience - investors, board members, senior leaders, or customers - on a topic you genuinely need them to act on. You will submit three things one week in advance: your Audience Contract, a one-page open/close pair with the seam test written out, and a written open loop with the sentence where you narrow it. On the day, you will deliver the talk and the panel will respond to your ask - they will either accept it, counter it, or ask what you want them to do, and all three are scored. You are assessed on the two ends of the talk and on what survives them: a talk with excellent content and a weak opening and close fails, and so does a talk with strong ends and no argument in the middle.

rubric.excellent: A single, clearly identifiable archetype chosen for reasons visible in the room: the stake appears in the first 20 to 30 seconds, the specific question or scene is planted with a detail only the speaker could know, and the opening is calibrated to the panel's actual state. The panel can restate the speaker's stake accurately afterwards.
rubric.adequate: The opening is professional and gets to a point, but the archetype is generic or unchosen - it reads as a reasonable default rather than a decision. The stake arrives, but late enough to have cost attention, or it is stated in generic terms that could fit any talk.
rubric.poor: The opening is a preamble - background, agenda, credentials, or a throat-clear - that consumes the first ninety seconds. The panel shows visible disengagement, and the speaker's category for the talk is set in the first thirty seconds and never revised.

rubric.dimension: The open loop and the management of curiosity
rubric.excellent: One specific question is planted in the first two minutes with an explicit promise of a payoff, narrowed once in the middle so the audience feels it closing, and closed visibly with the same words. The panel asks about the loop's subject before the talk ends.
rubric.adequate: A question or tension is set up and the talk stays coherent around it, but the plant and the resolution are not clearly connected; the payoff arrives without an explicit promise, or the loop is narrowed only in passing.
rubric.poor: Either no tension is set up and the talk is a flat report, or a question is raised and abandoned, or the talk opens with a mystery that is never resolved and the audience visibly stops expecting anything.

rubric.excellent: The opening contains a handle - a number with a denominator, a named person, a specific image - plus a small surprise and a stake tied to the panel's own situation. A week later a panelist can repeat the handle accurately, and the memorable element is also the true one.
rubric.adequate: The talk is engaging and pleasant, and the panel was attentive, but there is no handle: the substance is real and general, and a week later the panel remembers the topic rather than a specific sentence or image.
rubric.poor: Nothing in the talk is retained beyond its general subject. The content is generic, the stakes are abstract, and the opening could be lifted into any talk on any topic with no visible seam.

rubric.dimension: Closing construction: so what and callback
rubric.excellent: The close answers the panel's silent so-what in their language of consequence, then returns to the opening image or question with a changed meaning in a single line, and the two ends pass the seam test when read alone. The panel can state what changed for them and why the ending was worth reaching.
rubric.adequate: The close is coherent and does summarise the argument, but it is a recap rather than a conclusion, and the callback is either absent or functions as a reminder ('as I said at the start') rather than as a re-use with new meaning.
rubric.poor: The talk ends with a summary of slides, a thank-you, or 'any questions', and the panel cannot say what the talk wanted from them. The opening and the closing are unrelated, and the seam test fails - the ends do not stand alone together.

rubric.dimension: The ask and the last line
rubric.excellent: Exactly one ask, delivered as a standalone sentence in the final 60 seconds, naming a person or body, an action, a size, and a date, with a stated consequence if no decision is made. The final line passes the Last-Line Test: it stands alone, survives the speaker's absence, and is repeatable. The panel's response shows they understood what was being asked of them.
rubric.adequate: An ask exists and is reasonably clear, but one or more of the four elements is missing - a vague size, an undated request, or an implied rather than stated ask. The last line is weak but not empty: it points to the ask without being the ask itself.
rubric.poor: No identifiable ask, or two conflicting asks, or an ask buried in a paragraph of summary. The talk ends on a thank-you, on 'any questions?', or on an unfinished sentence, and the panel can be asked afterwards what was requested and cannot say.

rubric.dimension: Design integrity across the whole talk
rubric.excellent: The open, the middle, and the close form one argument: the plant is set up in the body, the loop is narrowed in the body, and the close pays off what the body earned. The seven minutes are one idea, and the panel can describe the whole talk in a single sentence.
rubric.adequate: The talk is coherent and the ends are consistent with the middle, but the body is a sequence of reasonable points rather than an argument, and some of the middle material would fit any version of this talk.
rubric.poor: The ends are bolted onto a middle that does not connect to them, or the talk is a list of unrelated items that happens to have an introduction and a summary. The panel leaves with a topic, not a position.

readingList.title: Resonate: Present Visual Stories that Transform Audiences
readingList.author: Nancy Duarte
readingList.why: The 'what is / what could be' structure, the sparkline, and the account of why presenters open with preamble and lose the room in the first minutes. Pairs directly with the five opening archetypes, the so-what close, and the rhyme work in this module.

readingList.title: Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die
readingList.author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
readingList.why: The clearest available treatment of what makes an idea concrete, surprising, and repeatable, including the guidance to build a story around a chosen moral and the rule of three. Read it alongside the memorable-versus-pleasant concept and the callback close.

readingList.title: Never Split the Difference: Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It
readingList.author: Chris Voss
readingList.why: Labelling - naming the other party's real concern before they do - and calibrated questions that invite the other side to solve for the constraint. This is the source of the labelling move in the Open Loop framework and in the renewal-call scenario. Pairs with m07 on Q&A and hostility.

readingList.title: How to Speak: How to Make Anyone Want to Listen
readingList.author: Ali Abdaal
readingList.why: The most current practitioner treatment of the hook-and-payoff structure for openings, and of why the first sentence determines whether there is a second one. A coaching text rather than a research text - useful precisely for its speed and its rehearsal drills.

readingList.title: Über das Behalten von erledigten und unerledigten Handlungen
readingList.author: Bluma Zeigarnik (1927), with the replication record from Pyc and Rawson (2009-2010)
readingList.why: The original interruption-effect work that the open loop is built on, together with the modern reanalysis that narrows the claim to resumable tasks and suggests unfinished goal persistence as the mechanism. Read it so you can state the evidence accurately in a room that knows the literature.

masteryChecklist: I can name the exact second my stake lands in an opening, and I can cut every sentence that could be moved to minute ten without damage.
I can choose between the five opening archetypes by matching the room's state and the raw material I actually hold, and I can say why the one I rejected was wrong for that room.
I can plant one open loop with a promised payoff, narrow it once in the middle, and close it visibly with the same words I opened with.
I can write a closing that answers the so-what in the audience's language of consequence rather than summarising my slides.
I can apply the Last-Line Test to my final sentence and explain why a talk should not end on a thank-you or on 'any questions'.
I can construct an explicit ask with a named person, action, size, and date, and I can state what happens if nobody acts.
I can write an opening and a closing that rhyme, and I can run the seam test to tell whether my talk has a spine or a list.
